**Audience**: a CV engineer leaving benchmarks for field latency / robustness. **Empirical first**: high lab mAP, low nighttime recall; a tracker that swaps IDs at crossings — then we name detection, SAM, MOT, stereo/LiDAR, edge deploy.

The "systems" counterpart of foundational vision: full application pipeline.

### What you will be able to do

-   Compare the two paradigms of object detection and choose a detector under the application constraint.
-   Rigorously evaluate a detector with mAP and read a public benchmark without being misled.
-   Distinguish semantic, instance and panoptic segmentation, and use a generic segmentation model such as SAM.
-   Implement multi-object tracking on a video sequence.
-   Exploit stereo and LiDAR for applied 3D perception.
-   Build and annotate a vision dataset, and measure its biases.
-   Deploy a model under constraint: ONNX export, quantization, edge execution.
-   Analyze the ethics, robustness and limits of an embedded vision system.

Since this module is published by the brochure without a SynapseS course description of its own, the closest official reference in the 2026-2027 catalog is the description of [CSC_52002_EP — "IA générative multimodale" (Multimodal Generative AI)](https://synapses.polytechnique.fr/catalogue/2026-2027/ue/19742/CSC-52002-EP-ia-generative-multimodale), a course unit of the (computer science) in-depth program of the LLGA track S2 with a vision focus: its official description presents multimodal generative AI — vision, audio, tactile information — as a paradigm shift that recomposes entire industries, from healthcare to automotive (tools such as Dall-E 3, Midjourney, GPT-Vision; autonomous driving). The official course proposes to go "beyond CNNs and transformers" and to cover the advanced topics of multimodal generative AI: from image generation to that of videos, sounds and robot actions. ### Where this course fits in the program

Module of period 2 of M1 (36 h, 4.5 ECTS), **mandatory according to the MSc&T brochure** (outside the recommended track in these materials); no dedicated SynapseS course description in the 2026-2027 catalog (period and assessment modalities: not communicated). It is the module that turns vision skills into deployment skills.

-   **Prerequisites** — [Image Analysis and Computer Vision](../m1p1-computer-vision/index.html) (P1), whose applied extension it is, and [Deep Learning](../m1p1-deep-learning/index.html) for CNNs and training; the review section covers convolution, CNNs and bounding boxes.
-   **Downstream modules** — the deployment chapter (ONNX, quantization, edge) directly prepares [ML Ops and LLM Engineering Principles](../m2-mlops-llm-engineering/index.html) (M2), and the industrial case studies anticipate the careers targeted by the master's program; vision systems also feed the multimodal pipelines of the [Multimodal Generative AI](../m1p2-multimodal-genai/index.html) module (same period).

### Course outline

-   **Review: convolution, CNNs, boxes** — the deep vision building blocks revisited before the application tasks.
-   **Object detection: the two paradigms** — one-stage and two-stage detectors, and their speed-accuracy trade-offs.
-   **Evaluation (mAP) and modern detectors** — measuring honestly first, then the panorama of recent architectures.
-   **Segmentation: semantic, instance, panoptic, SAM** — the three granularities of segmentation and the era of foundation models.
-   **Multi-object tracking** — following targets across a video, identities included.
-   **Applied 3D vision: stereo and LiDAR** — recovering depth for embedded applications.
-   **Data, benchmarks and annotation** — building the dataset and the protocol before chasing the model.
-   **Industrial case studies** — real deployments, with their constraints and lessons learned.
-   **Deployment: ONNX, quantization, edge** — fitting a model into an embedded compute budget.
-   **Ethics, robustness and limits** — biases, attacks and failure cases: what a deployed system must own up to.
-   **Exercises** and **References** — systematic training and sources to go further.

### How to study this module

-   Redo the review section if the P1 vision course is no longer fresh: detection and segmentation reuse convolution and boxes without revisiting them.
-   For every task, start from the metric before the model: understanding mAP or IoU first avoids 90 % of benchmark misinterpretations.
-   Reproduce a small end-to-end experiment on a public dataset: training, evaluation, then export — that is the heart of the module.
-   Concretely try ONNX export and quantization on a small model: the deployment chapter is understood with hands on the keyboard.
-   Prepare questions for the industrial case studies: that is where constraints, trade-offs and real careers play out.
-   Redo the exercises of each section before moving on to the next; they calibrate your expectations of what a deployed system can actually do.

::: note
[Note Extrapolons]{.tag} This module gives the master's program its "perception systems" building block: vision is the sensory input of multimodal pipelines and multimodal LLMs, and its embedded deployment foreshadows the practices of the [ML Ops and LLM Engineering Principles](../m2-mlops-llm-engineering/index.html) module (M2). Inspection, autonomous vehicles, robotics, imaging: the course's case studies are a dress rehearsal for the industrial careers targeted by the program.
:::

## 0. Review: convolution, CNNs, boxes {#ch0}

:::: recap
::: recap-title
L3 review — what is assumed known
:::

-   **Digital image**: an $H \times W$ grid of pixels with $C$ channels (3 in RGB), a tensor $x \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times H \times W}$; grayscale, resolution, sampling (cf. Signal Processing module, chapter 2).
-   **2D convolution**: $(I \* k)(u, v) = \sum_{i,j} I(u-i, v-j)\,k(i, j)$; properties (commutativity, association with the product), Sobel / low-pass counterparts, correlation vs convolution (cf. Signal Processing module, chapter 3).
-   **Convolutional networks**: receptive fields, weight sharing, pooling, the ResNet architecture (residual connections) — cf. Deep Learning module, chapter 4; attention and transformers — cf. Deep Learning module, chapter 6.
-   **Supervised learning**: gradient descent, SGD/Adam, overfitting, regularization, transfer learning and fine-tuning — cf. Deep Learning module, chapters 3 and 8; cross-validation, ROC curves — cf. the Machine Learning module.
::::

The P1 course "Image Analysis and Computer Vision" (CSC_51073_EP) laid the foundations: filtering, local features, projective geometry, reconstruction. The present module takes the **systems and applications** orientation: we build the complete pipeline of a vision product — from annotated data to a model deployed on constrained hardware — and study the building blocks industry actually uses (detectors, segmenters, trackers, 3D sensors, inference runtimes).

::: def
[Definition 0.1 — Bounding box and IoU]{.tag} A **bounding box** is an axis-aligned rectangle $b = (x_1, y_1, x_2, y_2)$ with $x_1 \< x_2$, $y_1 \< y_2$, encoding the top-left and bottom-right corners. For two boxes $a$ and $b$, let $A(a)$ denote the area of the rectangle. The **intersection-over-union** is $$\mathrm{IoU}(a, b) \;=\; \frac{\|a \cap b\|}{\|a \cup b\|} \;=\; \frac{\|a \cap b\|}{A(a) + A(b) - \|a \cap b\|},$$ where $\|\cdot\|$ denotes area. The intersection box has corners $(\max(x_1^a, x_1^b), \max(y_1^a, y_1^b))$ and $(\min(x_2^a, x_2^b), \min(y_2^a, y_2^b))$ if these coordinates are consistent, otherwise the intersection is empty and $\mathrm{IoU} = 0$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.2 — Properties of IoU]{.tag} For all axis-aligned boxes $a, b$: (i) $\mathrm{IoU}(a,b) \in [0, 1]$; (ii) $\mathrm{IoU}(a,b) = \mathrm{IoU}(b,a)$; (iii) $\mathrm{IoU}(a,b) = 1$ if and only if $a = b$ (up to equality of pixel sets); (iv) $\mathrm{IoU}(a,b) = 0$ if and only if the interiors of the two rectangles are disjoint.

::: proof
\(i\) The intersection area is a rectangle area, positive and bounded by each of the areas, so $0 \leq \|a \cap b\| \leq \min(A(a), A(b)) \leq \|a \cup b\|$. (ii) The intersection and union operations are symmetric. (iii) If $\mathrm{IoU} = 1$ then $\|a \cap b\| = \|a \cup b\|$, so $\|a \setminus b\| = \|b \setminus a\| = 0$ and the rectangles coincide; the converse is immediate. (iv) If the intersection is empty, the numerator is zero; conversely a non-empty intersection rectangle has strictly positive area, hence $\mathrm{IoU} \> 0$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 0.3 — An IoU computation]{.tag} Let the ground truth be $g = (0, 0, 10, 10)$ (area 100) and the prediction $p = (5, 5, 15, 15)$ (area 100). The intersection is the square $(5,5,10,10)$ of area 25, the union equals $100 + 100 - 25 = 175$, so $\mathrm{IoU}(g, p) = 25/175 \approx 0.143$: the prediction is rejected at the usual threshold $\tau = 0.5$. A prediction shifted by only 2 pixels, $p' = (2, 2, 12, 12)$, gives an intersection of 64 and a union of 136, i.e. $\mathrm{IoU} \approx 0.47$ — still below the threshold: on small objects the metric is unforgiving, which will justify the multiple thresholds of chapter 2.
:::

::: note
[Note — Position in the program]{.tag} This module is listed as a **mandatory course of the MSc&T brochure** (period 2); the brochure's reference instructor will be confirmed at the start of the period. The technical choices (detectors selected, lab datasets) will follow the industrial standards presented here: COCO for detection/segmentation, MOT for tracking, nuScenes/KITTI for 3D, MVTec AD for inspection.
:::

## 1. Object detection: the two paradigms {#ch1}

Concrete scene: an embedded detector that misses small objects for lack of multi-scale. This chapter sets the detection task.

::: note
[What breaks]{.tag} mAP alone without latency cost; too aggressive NMS; dataset without night / weather domain.
:::

::: def
[Definition 1.1 — The detection task]{.tag} Given an image $x$, produce a set $\{(b_i, c_i, s_i)\}_{i=1}^{N}$ where $b_i$ is a bounding box, $c_i$ a class among $K$ classes and $s_i \in [0,1]$ a confidence score. Unlike classification (cf. Deep Learning module, chapter 1), the output has variable cardinality: the number of objects is unknown and depends on the image content.
:::

### 1.1. The two-stage family: propose then refine

**Two-stage** detectors separate the generation of candidates from their classification:

-   **R-CNN** (2014): \~2000 candidate regions extracted by cluster-based segmentation (selective search), each crop goes through a CNN; slow (tens of seconds per image), but the proof of concept of the CNN in detection;
-   **Fast R-CNN** (2015): the whole image passes through the CNN once, candidates are projected into the feature space (RoI pooling); only a light classifier is applied per candidate;
-   **Faster R-CNN** (2015): candidates are produced by an integrated, end-to-end learned *Region Proposal Network* (RPN) — the canonical scheme;
-   **FPN** (2017): feature pyramid; small objects are detected on the high-resolution maps, large ones on the low-resolution maps.

::: def
[Definition 1.2 — Anchors]{.tag} For each cell of a feature map, the RPN predicts offsets with respect to a fixed set of $A$ reference rectangles — the **anchors** — produced by the Cartesian product of $S$ scales and $R$ aspect ratios (typically $S = 5$, $R = 3$, hence $A = 15$ anchors per position). The box regression encodes $$t_x = \frac{x - x_a}{w_a}, \quad t_y = \frac{y - y_a}{h_a}, \quad t_w = \log\frac{w}{w_a}, \quad t_h = \log\frac{h}{h_a},$$ where $(x_a, y_a, w_a, h_a)$ are the center and size of the anchor.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.3 — Why the logarithm for sizes]{.tag} The logarithmic parameterization makes the regression **scale invariant**: the same offset $t_w$ corresponds to the same size ratio. An error $\|t_w\| = \varepsilon$ means $w = w_a e^{\pm\varepsilon}$, i.e. a constant relative error rate; with a linear parameterization, the same absolute error would be negligible for a truck (600 px) and fatal for a distant pedestrian (10 px).

::: proof
With $t_w = \log(w / w_a)$, we have $w = w_a e^{t_w}$, so the relative error equals $\|e^{t_w} - 1\| \approx \|t_w\|$ at first order — independent of $w_a$. With a direct parameterization $\tilde t_w = w - w_a$, the relative error $\|\tilde t_w\| / w_a$ depends on $w_a$; fixing a homogeneous noise scale for all object sizes would require weighting by size class, and the loss would be dominated by large objects. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### 1.2. The single-stage family: everything in one pass

**Single-stage** detectors directly predict boxes and classes over a dense grid, in a single pass:

-   **YOLO** (2015): the image is cut into a $7 \times 7$ grid; each cell predicts 2 boxes + class probabilities; remarkable speed (45 images/s at the time), at the cost of coarser localization;
-   **SSD** (2016): multi-scale predictions via feature maps of decreasing resolutions, anchors per cell;
-   **RetinaNet** (2017): introduced the **focal loss** to correct the foreground/background imbalance (hundreds of thousands of easy anchors against a few objects), reconciling single-stage and two-stage accuracy.

::: def
[Definition 1.4 — Focal loss]{.tag} For per-anchor binary classification with logit $z$, predicted probability $p = \sigma(z)$ and label $y \in \{0, 1\}$: $$\mathrm{FL}(p) \;=\; -\alpha\,(1 - p_t)^{\gamma}\,\log(p_t), \qquad p_t = y\,p + (1 - y)(1 - p),$$ with balancing factor $\alpha \in [0,1]$ and **focusing** $\gamma \> 0$ (typically $\gamma = 2$). When $\gamma = 0$ and $\alpha = 0.5$, one recovers cross-entropy.
:::

The effect of the factor $(1 - p_t)^{\gamma}$ is to **divide the contribution of easy examples**: a background anchor classified at $p_t = 0.9$ has its loss reduced by a factor $0.1^2 = 0.01$; the rare hard examples (small $p_t$) keep an almost intact gradient. The gradient becomes $\frac{\partial \mathrm{FL}}{\partial z} = -\alpha\,(1-p_t)^{\gamma}\big(\gamma\, p_t \log p_t + 1 - p_t\big)\,\frac{\partial p_t}{\partial z}$: the magnitude concentrates on the decision boundary.

  Criterion             Two-stage (Faster R-CNN + FPN)          Single-stage (YOLO/SSD/RetinaNet)
  --------------------- --------------------------------------- ---------------------------------------------
  Principle             proposals then refined classification   dense prediction in one pass
  Accuracy (COCO mAP)   historically the high reference         comparable since RetinaNet and recent YOLOs
  Latency               higher (two passes + RoI)               low, suited to real time
  Small objects         good (FPN, aligned RoIs)                sensitive to input resolution
  Use cases             offline analysis, medical imaging       embedded, video, robotics

### 1.3. Non-maximum suppression (NMS)

Dense detectors emit many redundant boxes around the same object. **NMS** keeps the highest-scoring box and removes the ones that overlap it too much:

1.  sort the $N$ detections by decreasing score;
2.  take the first box $b$, add it to the kept ones;
3.  remove every box $b'$ such that $\mathrm{IoU}(b, b') \> \tau$ (typically $\tau = 0.5$);
4.  resume at step 2 with the remaining boxes, until exhaustion.

```python
import numpy as np

def nms(boxes, scores, tau=0.5):
    """boxes: (N,4) [x1,y1,x2,y2]; scores: (N,); returns the kept indices."""
    x1, y1, x2, y2 = boxes[:, 0], boxes[:, 1], boxes[:, 2], boxes[:, 3]
    areas = np.maximum(0, x2 - x1) * np.maximum(0, y2 - y1)
    order = scores.argsort()[::-1]          # sort by decreasing score
    keep = []
    while order.size > 0:
        i = order[0]
        keep.append(i)
        xx1 = np.maximum(x1[i], x1[order[1:]])
        yy1 = np.maximum(y1[i], y1[order[1:]])
        xx2 = np.minimum(x2[i], x2[order[1:]])
        yy2 = np.minimum(y2[i], y2[order[1:]])
        inter = np.maximum(0, xx2 - xx1) * np.maximum(0, yy2 - yy1)
        iou = inter / (areas[i] + areas[order[1:]] - inter)
        order = order[1:][iou <= tau]       # remove the overlapping ones
    return np.array(keep)
```

::: note
[Note — Limits of greedy NMS]{.tag} NMS is **greedy**: worst-case $O(N^2)$, it can remove a true detection that overlaps a distinct object (two people touching, aligned train cars). **Soft-NMS** (Bodla et al., 2017) replaces the binary removal with a score decay $s_i \mapsto s_i \cdot f(\mathrm{IoU})$ — linear or Gaussian — giving overlapping boxes a second chance; per-class NMS must be applied class by class, except in "class-agnostic" variants. The set-prediction detectors of chapter 2 replace NMS with a global, differentiable matching.
:::

## 2. Evaluation (mAP) and modern detectors {#ch2}

### 2.1. Precision, recall and AP — computed on an example

::: def
[Definition 2.1 — Precision, recall, AP and mAP]{.tag} For a given class, a detection is a **true positive** (TP) if $\mathrm{IoU}(\text{prediction}, \text{ground truth}) \geq \tau$ (*and* if that ground truth is not already matched); otherwise it is a false positive (FP); an undetected ground truth is a false negative (FN). Then $$\text{precision} = \frac{TP}{TP + FP}, \qquad \text{recall} = \frac{TP}{TP + FN} = \frac{TP}{\|\text{ground truths}\|}.$$ The **average precision** (AP) is the area under the precision-recall curve obtained by sweeping the score threshold; the COCO **mAP** averages the APs over 80 classes and over 10 IoU thresholds $\tau \in \{0.5,\, 0.55,\, \dots,\, 0.95\}$ — denoted $\mathrm{mAP}@[0.5{:}0.95]$.
:::

::: ex
[Example 2.2 — AP of one class by hand]{.tag} One class ("cat") with 3 ground truths and 5 detections sorted by decreasing score, evaluated at threshold $\tau = 0.5$:

  Rank   Score   Verdict   Cumulative TP   Precision    Recall
  ------ ------- --------- --------------- ------------ ------------
  1      0.95    TP        1               1/1 = 1.00   1/3 = 0.33
  2      0.90    FP        1               1/2 = 0.50   0.33
  3      0.85    TP        2               2/3 = 0.67   2/3 = 0.67
  4      0.70    FP        2               2/4 = 0.50   0.67
  5      0.40    TP        3               3/5 = 0.60   3/3 = 1.00

With "all-points" interpolation (precision clipped by the maximum to the right), the retained points are $(0.33; 1.00)$, $(0.67; 0.67)$ and $(1.00; 0.60)$, hence $$\mathrm{AP} \approx 0.33 \times 1.00 + 0.34 \times 0.67 + 0.33 \times 0.60 \approx 0.75.$$ The AP rewards *both* the ranking of the scores (an FP at high score is costly) and completeness; this is why it is more informative than a simple accuracy at a fixed threshold.
:::

::: note
[Note — Why multiple thresholds]{.tag} At $\tau = 0.5$, a detector can be right "loosely": averaging over $[0.5{:}0.95]$ penalizes mediocre localizations. COCO also publishes $\mathrm{mAP}_S, \mathrm{mAP}_M, \mathrm{mAP}_L$ by object size — a "globally" good industrial model can be very poor on small objects, a crucial point for video surveillance or microscopy.
:::

### 2.2. Without anchors: anchor-free detectors

Anchors impose an arbitrary grid of hypotheses. **Anchor-free** detectors directly predict, per pixel of the feature map: (i) a probability of being an object center (*centerness* / center heatmap, cf. **FCOS** and **CenterNet**) and (ii) regressions of the distances to the four edges. The decoding becomes: $$b = (x_c - l, \; y_c - t, \; x_c + r, \; y_c + b'),$$ where $(x_c, y_c)$ is the position of the central pixel and $l, t, r, b'$ the regressed distances — all of it without any reference box. Benefits: fewer hyperparameters (scales/ratios), no anchor/object imbalance, better on atypical shapes; cost: an NMS is still needed, and the center-to-ground-truth assignment requires zone rules (assignment by feature zone).

### 2.3. Detection as set prediction: DETR

::: def
[Definition 2.3 — DETR (DEtection TRansformer)]{.tag} DETR treats detection as a **set prediction** problem: a CNN extracts features, a transformer encoder-decoder (cf. Deep Learning module, chapter 6) produces $N$ *object queries* decoded into $N$ (box, class) pairs; training matches predictions and ground truths by **minimum-cost bipartite coupling** (Hungarian algorithm): $$\hat\sigma = \arg\min_{\sigma \in \mathfrak{S}_N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \Big( \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{box}}(b_i, g_{\sigma(i)}) + \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cls}}(c_i, y_{\sigma(i)}) \Big),$$ then applies a "set prediction"-type loss (Hungarian loss) on the optimal matching. Since the output is a learned *set* without redundancy, DETR removes NMS and anchors.
:::

::: note
[Note — Why DETR converges slowly, and the fix]{.tag} Global attention struggles to precisely localize small boxes (attention spreads over the whole image): DETR needed \~500 epochs. **Deformable DETR** replaces dense attention with *deformable attention* that samples only a small set of relevant points per query, speeding up convergence by an order of magnitude. The Hungarian matching is a minimum-cost assignment coupling — exactly the discrete transport seen in the Computational Optimal Transport module, chapters 1–2 (there solved by the Hungarian method rather than by Sinkhorn).
:::

### 2.4. The industrial YOLO ecosystem

  Version   Year   Key contribution                                                        Typical use
  --------- ------ ----------------------------------------------------------------------- -----------------------------
  YOLOv1    2016   single-pass dense prediction, real time                                 proof of concept
  YOLOv3    2018   multi-scale predictions (FPN), anchors per scale                        legacy surveillance
  YOLOv5    2020   tooling (ONNX/TF Lite export, S–X sizes), Ultralytics ecosystem         fast deployment
  YOLOv8+   2023   anchor-free heads, unified detection + segmentation + pose + tracking   current industrial standard

The important point for the engineer: these versions are less scientific revolutions than **training and tooling recipes** (mosaic augmentation, dynamic assignment loss, multi-format export). Knowing how to read a detector's changelog — which modules change, which data, which licenses (GPL for the Ultralytics line, Apache-2.0 for others) — is part of the module's skills.

## 3. Segmentation: semantic, instance, panoptic, SAM {#ch3}

### 3.1. Three granularities

  Task       Output                           Question answered                      Examples
  ---------- -------------------------------- -------------------------------------- ----------------
  Semantic   class map $H \times W$          "what is the class of this pixel?"     U-Net, DeepLab
  Instance   set of masks $(m_i, c_i, s_i)$   "which distinct objects?"              Mask R-CNN
  Panoptic   map of segmented identifiers     "'stuff' pixels + 'thing' instances"   Panoptic FPN

### 3.2. Semantic segmentation: from FCN to U-Net and DeepLab

-   **FCN** (2015): fully convolutional classification — the fully-connected layers become 1×1 convolutions, and *upsampling* (transposed) layers restore the resolution; dense output, end-to-end training;
-   **U-Net** (2015): symmetric encoder-decoder with **skip connections** that reinject the encoder's high-resolution details into the decoder; designed for medical imaging with few annotated images, and still the domain's reference;
-   **DeepLab** (v1→v3+): **dilated** (atrous) convolutions: a $3 \times 3$ kernel with dilation $d$ sees a neighborhood of size $2d+1$, enlarging the receptive field without losing resolution; the ASPP module (Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling) combines several dilations in parallel to capture several scales; v3+ adds a light decoder.

::: ex
[Example 3.1 — Dice and IoU of masks]{.tag} For a predicted binary mask $p$ and a ground truth $g$ (sets of pixels), the IoU is $\|p \cap g\| / \|p \cup g\|$ and the **Dice** $2\|p \cap g\| / (\|p\| + \|g\|)$. With $\|p\| = 1200$, $\|g\| = 1000$ and $\|p \cap g\| = 900$: IoU $= 900/1300 \approx 0.69$ and Dice $= 1800/2200 \approx 0.82$. One checks the identity $\mathrm{Dice} = 2\,\mathrm{IoU} / (1 + \mathrm{IoU})$: $2 \times 0.692 / 1.692 = 0.818$ — the two metrics are interchangeable as a ranking, but Dice looks "kinder": always specify the metric in a report.
:::

### 3.3. Instance segmentation: Mask R-CNN

**Mask R-CNN** (2017) extends Faster R-CNN: in parallel with the classification and box-regression heads, each region of interest receives a segmentation head that predicts a $28 \times 28$ binary mask (per class). The decisive detail is **RoI Align**: the original RoI pooling quantized the cell coordinates (rounding), shifting the features by a few tenths of a pixel — negligible for classification, disastrous for aligning a mask. RoI Align samples by bilinear interpolation at the real coordinates, without rounding: \~2 mask AP points gained from a mere numerical-precision fix — a fine engineering lesson.

### 3.4. Panoptic: a single metric

::: def
[Definition 3.2 — Panoptic Quality (PQ)]{.tag} Predicted segments and ground truths are matched per class with $\mathrm{IoU} \> 0.5$ (at-most-one-to-one coupling). With TP the set of matches, FP the unmatched predictions and FN the unmatched ground truths: $$\mathrm{PQ} \;=\; \underbrace{\frac{1}{\|\mathrm{TP}\|}\sum_{(p,g) \in \mathrm{TP}} \mathrm{IoU}(p, g)}_{\text{segmentation quality (SQ)}} \;\times\; \underbrace{\frac{\|\mathrm{TP}\|}{\|\mathrm{TP}\| + \tfrac12\|\mathrm{FP}\| + \tfrac12\|\mathrm{FN}\|}}_{\text{recognition quality (RQ = F1 score)}},$$ then averaged over the classes. PQ cleanly decouples "are the boundaries right?" (SQ) and "did I find the right objects?" (RQ).
:::

### 3.5. SAM: promptable segmentation

The **Segment Anything Model** (Meta, 2023) changes paradigm: instead of training a model per task, SAM learns a *general task* — produce a valid mask for any **prompt** (point, box, coarse mask, text to come):

-   **architecture**: a heavy image encoder (ViT, cf. Advanced Deep Learning module (P2), chapter 1) computed once per image; a light prompt encoder; a light mask decoder, re-runnable in real time (\~50 ms) for every prompt — the expensive-once / light-many-times separation is the "interactive" deployment pattern;
-   **data engine**: an assisted-annotation loop (model suggests, human corrects) at first, then semi-automatic then automatic annotation — culminating in SA-1B: 11 million licensed images, **1.1 billion masks**, 99 % automatic;
-   **usage**: zero-shot mask extraction, serving as a base for fine-tuning (medical, satellite), or as an annotation assistant — SAM closes the loop there: the model manufactures its own data.

## 4. Multi-object tracking {#ch4}

::: def
[Definition 4.1 — Multi-object tracking (MOT)]{.tag} Given a video stream, associate across frames the detections of the *same* physical object under a stable **track identifier**, while managing appearances, disappearances, occlusions and crossings. The dominant paradigm is **tracking-by-detection**: a detector (chapters 1–2) runs at every frame; the tracker reduces to the **association** problem between current detections and existing tracks.
:::

### 4.1. SORT: Kalman + Hungarian matching

**SORT** (2016) is the minimal tracker:

1.  each track carries a constant-velocity Kalman filter (state $[x, y, s, \dot x, \dot y, \dot s]$; the Kalman filter is recalled below);
2.  prediction: the boxes are extrapolated to the current frame;
3.  association: solve the bipartite coupling between predictions and detections with cost $1 - \mathrm{IoU}$ (Hungarian algorithm);
4.  the formed pairs update the filters (correction); tracks left unmatched for $T_{\text{max}}$ consecutive frames are destroyed; orphan detections create new tracks.

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Reminder — the Kalman filter in two equations
:::

Linear-Gaussian state model $x_t = F x_{t-1} + w$, observation model $z_t = H x_t + v$, white noises with covariances $Q, R$: $$\hat x_{t\|t-1} = F \hat x_{t-1\|t-1}, \quad P_{t\|t-1} = F P_{t-1\|t-1} F^\top + Q \quad (\text{prediction}),$$ $$K_t = P_{t\|t-1} H^\top (H P_{t\|t-1} H^\top + R)^{-1}, \quad \hat x_{t\|t} = \hat x_{t\|t-1} + K_t (z_t - H \hat x_{t\|t-1}) \quad (\text{correction}).$$ The gain $K_t$ weighs the prediction (motion) and the observation (detection) according to their uncertainties — cf. the Signal Processing module for the Bayesian interpretation.
::::

### 4.2. DeepSORT: adding appearance

In a crowd, two pedestrians who cross paths swap their boxes: IoU alone re-associates poorly. **DeepSORT** (2017) associates in two stages: (i) **cascade matching** favoring recently seen tracks, with a cost combining IoU *and* an **appearance embedding** distance — a small ReID (re-identification) network learns a descriptor $e_i \in \mathbb{R}^{128}$ invariant to pose/scale; (ii) IoU matching (as in SORT) for the rest. The "appearance memory" (a gallery of the last descriptors per track) resists long occlusions.

### 4.3. ByteTrack: don't throw away low-score detections

**ByteTrack** (2022) starts from a simple observation: during a partial occlusion, the detector often emits a *correct but low-confidence* detection — which classical pipelines discard at the threshold. The algorithm sketch:

1.  split the detections into high score ($\geq \tau_{\mathrm{high}}$, e.g. 0.5) and low score ($\tau_{\mathrm{low}} \leq s \< \tau_{\mathrm{high}}$);
2.  first matching: *active* tracks vs high-score detections, Hungarian coupling on a combined distance (IoU + appearance);
3.  second matching: tracks *still orphaned* vs low-score detections, coupling on IoU alone — the low-confidence boxes "carry" the track through the occlusion;
4.  tracks still orphaned are put on hold then destroyed; orphan high-score detections create tracks (never the low-score ones).

Result: notable MOTA/IDF1 gains *without any new detector* — association is a lever as profitable as perception.

### 4.4. Measuring a tracker

::: def
[Definition 4.2 — MOTA and IDF1]{.tag} $$\mathrm{MOTA} = 1 - \frac{\|\mathrm{FN}\| + \|\mathrm{FP}\| + \|\mathrm{ID\ switches}\|} {\sum_t \|\text{ground truths}_t\|}, \qquad \mathrm{IDF1} = \frac{2\,\mathrm{IDTP}}{2\,\mathrm{IDTP} + \mathrm{IDFP} + \mathrm{IDFN}},$$ where ID switches count identity flips (a tracker that "swaps" two people loses IDF1 even if its MOTA is good). MOTA mostly measures *detection*; IDF1 mostly measures *identity*; HOTA (2020) rebalances detection and association.
:::

::: note
[Note — In production]{.tag} Tracking imposes strong system constraints: per-frame latency (the tracker must fit in the budget, cf. chapter 8); robustness to detector dropouts (a missed frame); re-identification after leaving the field of view; and, in multi-camera settings, cross-camera association (pure ReID, with no IoU available). The two key building blocks — Hungarian coupling and the Kalman filter — are L3 classics; the modernity lies in the learned descriptors.
:::

## 5. Applied 3D vision: stereo and LiDAR {#ch5}

### 5.1. The pinhole model (reminder)

:::: recap
::: recap-title
L3 reminder — perspective projection
:::

A pinhole camera projects a 3D point $X = (X, Y, Z)$ (camera frame, $Z$ pointing forward) to $(u, v)$ in the image: $$\lambda \begin{pmatrix} u \\ v \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = K \,[\,R \mid t\,] \begin{pmatrix} X \\ Y \\ Z \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad K = \begin{pmatrix} f_x & 0 & c_x \\ 0 & f_y & c_y \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix},$$ with $K$ the **intrinsics** (focal lengths in pixels, optical center), $[R\|t]$ the **extrinsics** (camera pose); $\lambda = Z$. Calibration (OpenCV) estimates $K$ and the distortion (radial-tangential model) — cf. the P1 course for the complete geometry (Hartley & Zisserman).
::::

### 5.2. Stereo: disparity as a depth measurement

::: def
[Definition 5.1 — Disparity]{.tag} For a rectified stereo pair (coplanar images, horizontal epipolar lines, common focal length $f$, baseline $B$), a 3D point projects to $(u_L, v)$ on the left and $(u_R, v)$ on the right; the **disparity** is $d = u_L - u_R \geq 0$, measured in pixels.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.2 — Depth from disparity]{.tag} In the rectified setting, the depth of the point is $$Z = \frac{f \, B}{d}.$$

::: proof
The 3D point $(X, Y, Z)$ projects on the left to $u_L = fX/Z$ and on the right (optical center shifted by $B$ along $x$) to $u_R = f(X - B)/Z$. Taking the difference, $u_L - u_R = fB/Z$, i.e. $d = fB / Z$ and hence $Z = fB / d$. [∎]{.qed}
:::

Practical consequence: the depth uncertainty $\partial Z / \partial d = -fB/d^2 = -Z^2/(fB)$ **grows quadratically with distance** — stereo is precise up close, coarse far away; increasing $B$ or $f$ improves range at the price of the visible field and harder matchings.
::::

The classical stereo pipeline: (i) rectification; (ii) **cost volume** — for every left pixel and every candidate disparity $d$, a matching cost (census, SSD of descriptors) — this is an $H \times W \times D_{\max}$ volume; (iii) aggregation and regularization: **SGM** (Hirschmüller, 2008) aggregates costs along several directions (per-path dynamic programming) with discontinuity penalties — the industrial standard (baked into GPUs!); (iv) disparity map. Deep methods (**PSM-Net** and successors) learn the cost volume: 3D convolutions on descriptors stacked by disparity — exactly the same volume construction that the Multimodal GenAI module, chapter 3, exploits for other data.

### 5.3. LiDAR: point clouds

LiDAR emits pulses and measures time of flight: the output is a 3D point cloud ($x, y, z$, reflectivity), \~100k–2M points/s, accurate in distance (\~2 cm), sparse and irregular — *unstructured*: grid convolutions do not apply directly. Families of methods:

-   **PointNet** (2017): per point, a shared MLP; aggregation by global *max*; then an MLP. **Permutation invariance** comes from the max: the global descriptor does not depend on the order of the points — cf. the proposition below;
-   **Voxels / pillars**: discretize space (VoxelNet) or only the ground plane (PointPillars: vertical columns), aggregate the point features there, then run a 2D/3D CNN on the resulting grid;
-   **Center detection**: CenterPoint projects everything into bird's eye view (BEV) and detects objects by their center (heatmap + size/rotation regression) — the anchor-free formulation of chapter 2, transposed to a 2D "top-down view".

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.3 — The global max is permutation invariant]{.tag} Let $h(X) = \mathrm{max}_{i=1..n} \mathrm{MLP}(x_i)$ be PointNet's global descriptor. For every permutation $\pi$ of $\{1, \dots, n\}$: $h(x_{\pi(1)}, \dots, x_{\pi(n)}) = h(x_1, \dots, x_n)$.

::: proof
The MLP is applied pointwise: the set $\{\mathrm{MLP}(x_i)\}$ is unchanged by permutation (only the enumeration order changes). The per-coordinate maximum of a set does not depend on the enumeration order, hence the equality. Note that a sum or an average would have the same property; the max is preferred because it selects one "witness" per coordinate and avoids the information smoothing of averages. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### 5.4. Multi-sensor fusion in bird's eye view

Cameras provide semantics (classes, traffic lights, signs) but only indirect depth; LiDAR provides geometry but poor semantics. Modern architectures fuse **in BEV**: every sensor is brought into a common top-down frame where detection, tracking and trajectory prediction combine. **BEVFormer** (2022): image features are "queried" in BEV space by spatial cross-attention (every BEV cell queries the pixels along its view pillar), with temporal attention toward the previous BEV map — tracking becomes implicit. The following table summarizes the sensor trade-offs:

  Sensor       Output               Density          Weather/light   Cost     Role
  ------------ -------------------- ---------------- --------------- -------- ---------------------
  Camera       dense RGB            high             sensitive       low      semantics
  LiDAR        3D cloud             medium, sparse   robust          high     geometry
  Radar (4D)   targets + velocity   low              very robust     medium   motion, bad weather

## 6. Data, benchmarks and annotation {#ch6}

### 6.1. The reference datasets

  Dataset      Year    Content                                                  Annotations              Use
  ------------ ------- -------------------------------------------------------- ------------------------ ---------------------------------------
  ImageNet     2009–   14M images, 22k classes                                  labels                   pretraining (DL reminder ch. 8)
  COCO         2014–   330k images, 80 classes                                  boxes, masks, captions   detection, segmentation, standard mAP
  KITTI        2012    urban scenes (camera + LiDAR)                            3D boxes, disparity      stereo, embedded 3D detection
  nuScenes     2019    1000 scenes, 1.4M images, 6 cameras + 1 LiDAR + radars   3D boxes, tracks         complete autonomous driving
  Waymo Open   2019–   \~2000 scenes, 5 LiDAR + 5 cameras                       3D boxes, tracking       large-scale 3D benchmark
  MVTec AD     2019    5k industrial images, 15 categories                      anomaly masks            inspection (chapter 7)

### 6.2. The cost of annotation

A COCO box costs from a few seconds to a minute; a polygon mask, much more; a 3D LiDAR box at 25 Hz over 20 objects, several minutes with dedicated tooling. Three industrial levers:

-   **assisted annotation**: a pretrained model proposes, the human corrects — the SA-1B loop of chapter 3 is its large-scale version; an additional benefit: **active learning** only has annotated the examples where the model is uncertain;
-   **synthetic data**: procedural 3D rendering with *domain randomization* (random textures, lighting to force invariance); the P2 module "Image Synthesis" (brochure) covers rendering; sim2real remains the hard part;
-   **augmentation**: geometric (cropping, rotation, mosaic) and photometric (color, blur, noise); caution: geometric transformations must transform the boxes/masks *and* the metadata (rotation → bounding boxes of the rotated masks).

### 6.3. Evaluation pitfalls

::: note
[Note — The three classic pitfalls]{.tag} **(1) Data leakage**: near-duplicate images between train and test (video sequences); always split by video/scene, not by image. **(2) Long-tail imbalance**: the global mAP masks rare classes — look at the per-class APs; the training data must be resampled or reweighted (cf. focal loss, chapter 1). **(3) Domain shift**: a COCO model collapses on your production cameras (angle, compression, weather); plan from the protocol stage for a "shadow" set of unseen real data, and drift monitoring in operation (chapter 8).
:::

## 7. Industrial case studies {#ch7}

### 7.1. Industrial inspection (quality control)

Inspecting parts (scratches, cracks, contamination) on a production line: controlled lighting (strobe, dark background), imposed cadence (decisions per second), and — the major specificity — **very few defect examples**. Hence the move to **unsupervised** methods: learn *normality* (autoencoders, feature distances; cf. Deep Learning module, chapter 7, for autoencoders) and raise an alert on deviation; the **MVTec AD** dataset is the reference benchmark (15 categories: screws, textiles, wood, bottles…, with pixel-level defect masks). Metrics: image-level detection (AUROC) and defect segmentation (pixel AUROC, PRO). Constraints: an error is asymmetrically costly (false rejection = yield loss; missed defect = product recall); the threshold is tuned on business cost, not on 0.5.

::: ex
[Example 7.1 — Tuning a threshold on costs]{.tag} Let an anomaly score $s \in [0,1]$; false rejection costs €1 (manual re-inspection), missed defect costs €100 (product recall). At the operating point (FP rate $= 4\,\%$ on healthy parts, FN rate $= 2\,\%$ on defective parts, real defect rate 0.5 %): expected cost for 10,000 parts $$10\,000 \times \big[0.995 \times 0.04 \times 1 + 0.005 \times 0.02 \times 100\big] = 10\,000 \times (0.0398 + 0.01) \approx 498\ \text{euros}.$$ Lowering the threshold (more sensitive) increases FPs but reduces FNs: redo the computation and choose the threshold at the cost minimum — the right engineering metric is a cost, not an accuracy.
:::

### 7.2. Autonomous driving

The typical perception pipeline of a SAE level 2+ to 4 vehicle:

1.  multi-camera **detection/segmentation** (chapters 1–3);
2.  camera/LiDAR/radar **fusion** in BEV (chapter 5);
3.  **tracking and prediction** of agents (chapter 4 + trajectory models);
4.  **planning** (out of scope — cf. the Reinforcement Learning module for the MDP formalization);
5.  **system monitoring**: redundancy, diagnostics, degraded mode.

Engineering lessons: *corner cases* dominate the cost (roadworks, flashing lights, overturned trailers); closed benchmarks (nuScenes) are saturated and correlate poorly with real kilometers; safety imposes latency guarantees (chapter 8) and traceability (version of the model, the dataset, the threshold).

### 7.3. Medical imaging

Organ/lesion segmentation (U-Net is still the backbone, chapter 3), cell counting, fracture detection. Specificities: rare and costly data (clinicians), DICOM formats (metadata, windowing), strict clinical validation, regulation (medical CE marking); the metric is per-structure Dice and inter-observer consistency *is* the reachable ceiling — a Dice above human agreement is suspicious; the models are assistance tools (CAD — computer-aided diagnosis), not decision makers.

### 7.4. Other domains (summary)

-   **retail**: planograms (products on shelves), customer flows (anonymous counting);
-   **agriculture**: weed detection for targeted spraying (drone, embedded);
-   **sports**: player/ball tracking (chapter 4 at scale), tactical statistics;
-   **satellite**: building/road detection, deforestation masks — with domain randomization and multispectral imaging as a bonus.

## 8. Deployment: ONNX, quantization, edge {#ch8}

### 8.1. The deployment pipeline

From notebook to product, the canonical steps:

1.  **export**: the trained model (PyTorch) is exported as a frozen graph — **ONNX** (Open Neural Network Exchange), a common format accepted by most runtimes;
2.  **graph optimization**: operator fusion (conv + batchnorm → single conv; conv + activation), dead-layer elimination, kernel selection;
3.  **targeted compilation**: TensorRT (NVIDIA), Core ML (Apple), TF Lite / LiteRT (mobile), OpenVINO (Intel) — these generate hardware-specialized engines;
4.  **calibration/quantization**: move to INT8 (below);
5.  **measurement**: P50/P99 latency, throughput, memory, energy — on the target hardware, never on the development workstation alone.

```python
import torch

model = DetectorWrapper()          # PyTorch, eval mode
model.eval()
dummy = torch.randn(1, 3, 640, 640)

torch.onnx.export(
    model, dummy, "detector.onnx",
    input_names=["image"], output_names=["boxes", "scores", "labels"],
    dynamic_axes={"image": {0: "batch"},                # variable batch
                  "boxes": {0: "batch", 1: "num_boxes"}},  # variable N
    opset_version=17)              # recent opset for special ops

# runtime side: onnxruntime (CPU/GPU), TensorRT, Core ML...
import onnxruntime as ort
sess = ort.InferenceSession("detector.onnx", providers=["CPUExecutionProvider"])
boxes, scores, labels = sess.run(None, {"image": dummy.numpy()})
```

### 8.2. INT8 quantization

::: def
[Definition 8.1 — Affine quantization scheme]{.tag} To a floating tensor $x$ we associate a signed 8-bit integer via $$Q(x) = \mathrm{clip}\!\left(\mathrm{round}\!\left(\frac{x}{s}\right) + z,\; -128,\; 127\right), \qquad x \approx s\,(Q(x) - z),$$ with the **scale** $s \> 0$ and the **zero point** $z$ chosen by calibration (min-max of the activations on a representative sample, or percentile to limit the effect of extreme values). The weights are quantized once and for all; the activations are quantized at runtime.
:::

::: note
[Note — PTQ vs QAT]{.tag} **Post-training quantization** (PTQ): fast, no retraining, sufficient for many CNNs; **quantization-aware training** (QAT, Jacob et al. 2018): during training the quantization is simulated with fake operations (rounding on the forward pass, exact gradients on the backward pass — *straight-through estimator*), so the model learns to be robust to rounding; this is the solution when PTQ degrades too much (sensitive architectures, small models). Typical benefit: memory ÷4 (FP32→INT8) and throughput ×2–4 on targets with INT8 kernels — at the price of a few tenths of a mAP point to monitor.
:::

### 8.3. Compressing: pruning and distillation

-   **pruning**: zero out the lowest-magnitude weights (unstructured pruning — no gain without a sparse library) or whole channels (structured — actually accelerates); follow the accuracy/size curve;
-   **knowledge distillation** (Hinton et al., 2015): a small *student* imitates the output distribution of a large *teacher* — the loss combines the ground truth and the KL divergence with the teacher's logits "softened" by a temperature $T$: $$\mathcal{L} = \alpha\, \mathrm{CE}(y, z_s) + (1 - \alpha)\, T^2\, \mathrm{KL}\!\big(\mathrm{softmax}(z_t / T)\,\\|\,\mathrm{softmax}(z_s / T)\big)$$ (covered in detail in the Advanced Deep Learning module (P2), chapter 6).

### 8.4. Latency budgets and profiling

::: ex
[Example 8.2 — Budget of a "real-time detection" application]{.tag} 30 fps camera → 33.3 ms per-frame budget. Typical breakdown on an embedded module (Jetson Orin class): acquisition + decoding 3 ms; preprocessing (resizing, normalization, NV12→RGB) 4 ms; INT8 inference 18 ms; post-processing (NMS + rendering) 3 ms; margin 5 ms. Three lessons: (i) pre/post-processing is not negligible — keep it on the GPU (DALI/TensorRT-PLUGIN pipeline) if possible; (ii) target P99 latency (worst frame, with numerous detection batches), not the average; (iii) if the budget bursts, the levers in industrial order: input resolution ↓, smaller model (distillation), INT8, skip-frame + interpolation (detection at 15 Hz, tracking at 30 Hz — chapter 4 exists precisely for that).
:::

### 8.5. Operations, drift and privacy

-   **monitoring**: log score distributions, detection rates, "world" alerts (dirty camera, night); detect domain drift and plan retraining (the data loop of chapter 6);
-   **privacy**: process *on-device* as much as possible (no image leaves the sensor); if a stream is sent: blurring/anonymization of faces and plates (…detected by… the models of chapter 3!), minimal retention;
-   **versioning**: model + code + data + thresholds = a reproducible artifact — the methodology of the Advanced Deep Learning module (P2), chapter 8 applies mutatis mutandis.

## 9. Ethics, robustness and limits {#ch9}

### 9.1. Adversarial examples

Small imperceptible perturbations change the prediction. The simplest attack — **FGSM** — moves the input one step in the direction of the loss gradient: $$x_{\mathrm{adv}} = x + \varepsilon\, \mathrm{sign}\!\left(\nabla_x \mathcal{L}(\theta, x, y)\right),$$ with $\varepsilon$ on the order of 2–8/255. In detection, stickers glued to a sign can make an object disappear from the output; defenses range from adversarial training (min-max over perturbations) to bound-based certification — an overview is given in the Machine Learning module; the engineer mainly remembers: a model embedded in a product *can be targeted*, and robustness is tested (attack toolboxes) before deployment.

### 9.2. Bias and fairness of vision systems

-   **representation bias**: mostly North American/European datasets → performance drops in other contexts (streets, clothing, objects); the "Gender Shades" report documented accuracy gaps in detection by skin tone; in practice: break the evaluation down by subgroup (cf. Machine Learning module);
-   **surveillance and biometrics**: mass facial recognition is restricted/banned in several jurisdictions; the European AI regulation (AI Act, 2024) classifies remote biometric identification among high-risk or prohibited uses; anonymize *before* storage;
-   **consent**: scraped data (LAION etc.) and image rights; prefer clearly licensed datasets and document provenance (data cards).

### 9.3. Fundamental limits to know

::: note
[Note — What models do not "understand"]{.tag} **Compositionality**: a detector can see "a person" and "a bicycle" without inferring "a person *on* a bicycle" — relations require other formalisms (scene graphs; cf. Graph ML module). **Multimodal hallucination**: captioners describe absent objects (cf. Multimodal GenAI module, chapter 8). **Out of distribution**: snow, night, a new sensor — the displayed confidence is not calibrated outside the training distribution. **Causality**: vision correlates, it does not explain — a decision system must separate perception from decision (autonomous driving, chapter 7).
:::

## Exercises {#ex}

1.  **IoU and thresholds.** Compute the IoU between $g = (10, 10, 40, 60)$ and $p = (20, 5, 55, 50)$; determine the maximum offset $\delta$ in $x$ of a prediction identical to $g$ to stay above $\tau = 0.75$.
2.  **NMS by hand.** Five detections of the same class, scores 0.9; 0.85; 0.8; 0.75; 0.7, box 2 overlapping box 1 (IoU 0.6), box 3 overlapping box 1 (IoU 0.3) and box 4 overlapping box 3 (IoU 0.8). Give the boxes kept at $\tau = 0.5$ then at $\tau = 0.7$ with linear Soft-NMS ($s \leftarrow s(1 - \mathrm{IoU})$); comment on the "two objects stuck together" case.
3.  **AP.** With 4 ground truths and the sorted detections (TP, TP, FP, FP, TP, TP): draw the precision-recall curve, compute the all-points interpolated AP, then verify that moving the two FPs to the head of the list (FP, FP, TP, …) makes AP drop — why does the order of the scores matter?
4.  **Focal loss.** Show that for $\gamma = 2$, an easy anchor ($p_t = 0.95$) receives a weight $361$ times smaller than a hard anchor ($p_t = 0.3$); compute the ratio for plain cross-entropy and conclude.
5.  **Hungarian coupling.** Three tracks $T_1, T_2, T_3$, three detections $D_1, D_2, D_3$, costs $1-\mathrm{IoU}$: $T_1\!: (0.1,\ 0.8,\ 0.9)$, $T_2\!: (0.9,\ 0.2,\ 0.7)$, $T_3\!: (0.8,\ 0.9,\ 0.3)$. Solve the minimum-cost assignment by hand and compare with the greedy assignment — in which case do they differ?
6.  **Stereo depth.** Camera $f = 700$ px, baseline $B = 0.5$ m; compute the disparity of an object at 10 m, then the depth uncertainty if disparity is measured to ±0.25 px; at what distance does the uncertainty exceed 1 m?
7.  **PointNet.** Replace the max by an average in proposition 5.3: does the invariance hold; build two clouds with the same average but very different contents and conclude on the "selectivity" of the max.
8.  **PQ.** One image: 4 ground-truth segments, 3 predicted with matched IoUs 0.9; 0.8; 0.6 plus one FP; one FN. Compute SQ, RQ then PQ; redo with IoU 0.7 everywhere and comment on the decomposition.
9.  **Quantization.** A weight tensor has min −0.82 and max 0.55; give the scale and zero point (asymmetric 8-bit min-max scheme), quantize −0.1 and 0.3, dequantize, compute the relative error — why can a 99.9th percentile help?
10. **Real-time budget.** An application must detect at 25 fps on hardware where FP32 inference takes 58 ms and INT8 21 ms; preprocessing 5 ms, post-processing 4 ms. Does a single inference per frame fit? Propose two strategies (skip-frame + tracking; resolution reduction ÷1.4 with cost in $s^2$) and quantify their trade-offs.
11. **Data choice.** For a vehicle-counting system on a European road (day/night, rain), propose: a starting training set, a splitting protocol, an augmentation plan, a subgroup evaluation method, and two monitoring metrics in production.
12. **Project.** Complete pipeline on a free set (a COCO subset or public drone images): fine-tuning of a modern YOLO, ONNX export, INT8 quantization, latency/mAP measurement before/after, then a one-page report in "industrial datasheet" format (error costs included, cf. example 7.1).
